items.why: The negative wording is awkward and tests a plainly repeated phrase rather than deeper comprehension.
The two uses of “he” make it unclear whether the question asks about the speaker or the earlier messenger.
The summary explicitly credits David and his men, though Jonathan’s individual victory creates a useful distinction.
Tracking “him” back to the officer is clear and meaningfully distinguishes the two men.
The old prophet requests the donkey and then clearly mounts it after his sons saddle it.
“First covenant” clearly distinguishes the three-party covenant from the following one.
The sequence clearly places Jotham’s succession after Uzziah’s burial.
The stated reason is clear, but being hurried out is also an immediate plausible reason for leaving.
The king’s quoted scenario clearly says capture comes before entry into the city.
The men explicitly reject staying and entering the city, then decide to surrender at the Aramean camp.
The ordering of the two battles makes Sibbekai the first killer, though “who kills first” is slightly unnatural.
“The news” is a vague key, and the question does not ask readers to identify what was actually reported.
The command “Seize him” clearly targets the man of God rather than the speaking king.
The passage directly states that Azariah and the other priests followed Uzziah into the temple.
The quoted plan clearly contrasts eating one child today with the other child tomorrow.
Zechariah is directly identified as Uzziah’s instructor in fearing God.
The reply to the officer is identifiable, but “in reply to the doubt” requires careful dialogue tracking.
The man directly explains that the Lord’s command prevents him from accepting the offer.
The event immediately before Paul leaves is clearly his talking until daylight.
The sentence clearly orders mobilizing before marching and laying siege, though the task is simple sequencing.
The nearest acting subject, Jehoiada, clearly gives the stored weapons to the commanders.
The final sentence explicitly identifies the accusers as those ordered to present the case.
The purpose is plainly to make Uzziah king, though “take” sounds less natural than the excerpt’s action.
“Under their command” clearly refers to the 2,600 family leaders rather than the muster officials.
Following the pronouns across the departure clearly identifies the man of God as the lion’s victim.
The officer is explicitly put at the gate and then trampled there by the people.
The two off-duty companies are explicitly assigned this task, but the long command makes the distinction demanding.
Standard letter formatting clearly identifies Claudius Lysias as writer and Felix as recipient.
Abishai rescues David by striking the threatening Philistine, so the target is unmistakable.
After recognizing their wrongdoing, the men explicitly decide to report immediately to the palace.
Paul’s quoted instruction directly says that the young man has something to tell the commander.
The report to the king immediately precedes the people’s plundering in the narrative.
The pronouns consistently refer to Uzziah, though “love of soil” makes the question slightly artificial.
“My son” clearly identifies the speaking woman’s child as the one eaten first.
The king requests prayer and the next sentence explicitly says the man of God intercedes.
The three groups God helps Uzziah against are explicitly listed and distinct from the tribute-paying Ammonites.
The prophet first brings the body to his city and only afterward places it in his tomb.
Joash is clearly the child hidden with his nurse, while his father Ahaziah is already dead.
The passage explicitly links the city’s calm to Athaliah’s death, not merely to the people’s rejoicing.
The commander calls two centurions and gives them the order to prepare the larger force.
The Arameans explicitly imagine the Hittite and Egyptian kings attacking, although Israel’s king supposedly hired them.
“This murderer” most plausibly means the king, but the nearby messenger and shifting speakers make the referent difficult.
Within the old prophet’s claimed message, “him” refers to the man of God who is to return and eat.
The sentence directly connects Paul’s prolonged speaking with his plan to leave the next day.
The contrast with the cavalry supports the soldiers, but “soldiers” can naturally include the cavalry.
The attacked plural group is the seven sons, who clearly flee after the possessed man beats them.
“On the items’ arrival” is not stated, and illnesses are cured while spirits leave, making the wording artificial.
The conspirators ask the council to petition the commander, who is the one expected to bring Paul.
After bringing the scrolls together, the practitioners immediately burn them in public.
The explicit sword order targets followers, but the woman is also taken out and put to death, inviting two answers.
Athaliah hears the noise before going to the crowd and only sees the king after arriving.
The plot awaits the commander’s consent, but the actual attack also depends on Paul being brought near the ambush.
The warning is directly addressed to the man of God and refers to his body and ancestors.
The prophecy explicitly names Josiah as the person who will sacrifice the priests on the altar.
